recent_posts.title: Setting Up Claude Code Agent Teams With Wsl2 and Tmux on Windows
recent_posts.summary: A step-by-step setup guide for running Claude Code agent teams on Windows using WSL2 and tmux. Covers enabling WSL2, installing Ubuntu and dependencies, installing Claude Code, configuring tmux for multi-pane agent visibility, symlinking the .claude config between Windows and WSL, enabling the experimental agent teams feature, and launching Claude inside a tmux session.

recent_posts.title: Optimizing AI Agents with Progressive Disclosure
recent_posts.summary: AI coding agents waste precious context window space when given too much information upfront. Applying the Progressive Disclosure principle — revealing complexity incrementally — to agent design means keeping AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files minimal (like a table of contents), writing skill descriptions as short selectors rather than full manuals, and using file references so agents fetch detail only when needed. The same discipline applies to MCP server tool descriptions. The result is a higher signal-to-noise ratio in the context window, leading to better agent responses.

recent_posts.title: How AI agents amplify the two fundamental ways software developers fail
recent_posts.summary: Software developers fail in two ways: building the thing wrong (technical execution flaws like bugs, security issues, poor architecture) or building the wrong thing (correct execution of the wrong problem). AI coding agents like Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code amplify both failure modes dramatically. They can generate buggy code at scale and execute on vague or misaligned specifications with speed and confidence, compounding waste far faster than human teams. The solution isn't to avoid agents but to invest more heavily in clear requirements, automated quality gates, frequent human review, stakeholder feedback loops, and outcome-based measurement rather than output-based measurement.

recent_posts.title: Claude Throttling and the Cloud
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic confirmed in March 2026 that it has been throttling Claude session limits during weekday peak hours (5 AM–11 AM Pacific), causing heavy users to exhaust their quotas faster than expected. The throttling affects roughly 7% of users—primarily Pro and Max subscribers doing token-intensive work like coding or running agents—while API users paying per token are unaffected. The root cause is a combination of real infrastructure constraints (specialized AI accelerator chips like NVIDIA H100s, AWS Trainium2, and Google TPUs are physically scarce and expensive) and unsustainable unit economics (Anthropic has spent over $10 billion on inference and training while generating only $5 billion in cumulative revenue). A simultaneous bug in Claude Code's prompt caching system caused 10–20x token overconsumption, compounding the problem. The situation exposes a fundamental tension between the traditional cloud promise of elastic infinite scale and the reality of frontier AI inference, where each token requires fixed GPU compute that cannot be provisioned on demand. Practical advice for developers includes scheduling batch jobs during off-peak hours, preferring API access over subscriptions for production workloads, and monitoring token consumption closely.

recent_posts.title: Build vs buy applied to brand identity and business differentiation
recent_posts.summary: Applying the classic software 'build vs. buy' decision to brand identity and business strategy. The core argument is that businesses should invest in building and owning the things that differentiate them in customers' eyes, while outsourcing or buying commodity solutions for everything else. Uses Apple vs. Walmart as a contrast, and Spotify as an example of a company that must own its user experience as a core brand asset. Limited resources mean you can't build everything, so focus custom effort on what makes you unique.

recent_posts.title: .NET Conf Most Popular Sessions Tool
recent_posts.summary: Steve Smith (Ardalis) built a CLI tool using .NET 10's new `dnx` feature to pull and display the most popular .NET Conf sessions from YouTube by view count for each year since 2021. The tool is distributed via NuGet and runnable with `dnx ardalis dotnetconf-stats`. The post also shares the top 10 session rankings for 2021–2025, noting that Clean Architecture sessions have consistently ranked in the top 3 every year. It explains why the author keeps presenting on Clean Architecture (sustained high demand) and introduces `dnx` as a convenient way to distribute and run .NET CLI utilities directly from NuGet without local installation.

recent_posts.title: AI tool pricing is investor-subsidized and a major price correction is coming
recent_posts.summary: AI tools like Claude, Copilot, and Cursor are currently priced far below their actual compute costs, subsidized by hundreds of billions in investor capital. Anthropic spends roughly $180/month to serve a developer on a $100-200/month plan. OpenAI lost $12 billion in a single quarter. Hyperscalers are committing ~$700B in AI infrastructure capex in 2026 alone. The author argues this pricing is unsustainable and predicts agentic AI subscriptions will increase 10x-100x by end of 2027. Businesses making irreversible decisions—like laying off engineers in favor of AI agents—based on today's artificially low rates face serious risk. The recommended approach is treating AI adoption as a portfolio decision: maintain engineering capability, instrument AI costs now, and avoid over-dependence on any single AI service.

recent_posts.title: Use Asciinema and Powersession on Windows
recent_posts.summary: A guide to recording terminal sessions on Windows using Asciinema and PowerSession. Since the Asciinema CLI doesn't natively support Windows, the Rust-based PowerSession-rs tool fills the gap by capturing terminal sessions into .cast files. The post covers installation, self-hosting the Asciinema JavaScript player alongside the .cast files, and a quick demo using a NuGet CLI tool.

recent_posts.title: Llms Need Mark as Answer
recent_posts.summary: LLMs need explicit user feedback mechanisms similar to Stack Overflow's "mark as answer" feature to identify which responses successfully solve problems. Without quality signals indicating whether conversations led to solutions, AI models training on user interactions cannot distinguish helpful responses from unhelpful ones. This feedback loop is critical for continued model improvement as traditional training data sources like Stack Overflow decline in activity.

recent_posts.summary: Steve Smith (Ardalis) reflects on 2025, sharing metrics across blogging (14 articles, 255k page views—down 50% likely due to AI), social media growth (16.5k YouTube subscribers, 15.8k LinkedIn followers), and open source work including Specification v9 release. He spoke at 6 conferences including a 5-in-4-weeks European tour, maintained several popular GitHub repositories (CleanArchitecture at 18k stars), but didn't publish new courses or books due to client work demands.
